Netflix: Data Exploration & Visualisation¶

What should Netflix produce next, and where should it grow?¶

Author: Guntuku Hariprasad  |  Dataset: 8,807 Netflix titles (movies & TV shows), catalogue snapshot up to 25 Sep 2021 Tools: Python, pandas, NumPy, Matplotlib, Seaborn

Executive summary (for business leaders)¶

What we found Number behind it
The catalogue is movie-heavy, but the mix is shifting towards TV 70% movies / 30% TV overall; TV share of new additions rose from 25% (2018) to 34% (2021)
For the newest releases, TV now beats movies Titles released in 2021: 315 TV shows vs 277 movies
Content growth peaked in 2019 and slowed during 2020–21 2,016 titles added in 2019 → 1,879 in 2020
Netflix is an adult-first library 45.6% of titles are rated for adults (TV-MA / R / NC-17); only 6.5% are made for little kids
Three markets supply 59% of the catalogue United States (3,690), India (1,046), United Kingdom (806)
Each country has a distinct content "personality" India = 92% movies (dramas, Bollywood stars); Japan & South Korea = majority TV (anime, K-dramas)
Fast-rising newcomer markets Nigeria (1 → 42 titles/yr, 2018→2020), Egypt (3 → 54); Japan & South Korea up 70–80%
Most TV shows never get past season 1 67% of TV shows have exactly 1 season
The sweet-spot movie is ~1.5–2 hours Half of all movies run 87–114 min (median 98 min)
Friday and the 1st of the month are the launch days 28% of titles added on a Friday; 2,212 titles added on the 1st

Top recommendations (detailed in Section 13): invest more in original TV series (especially international dramas, crime and kids' shows); build local-language content hubs in India, Japan, South Korea and fast-growing markets like Nigeria and Egypt; keep films around 90–110 minutes; release big shows on Fridays in July or December; and grow the family/kids slate, which is under-represented today.

1. Problem statement & approach¶

Business problem. Netflix (222M+ subscribers) must decide which type of shows and movies to produce or license and how to grow in different countries. Every content rupee/dollar is a bet; this analysis turns the current catalogue into evidence for those bets.

Questions this study answers

  1. What is the movie vs TV-show mix, and is Netflix focusing more on TV in recent years?
  2. How has the number of titles released/added changed over the last 20–30 years?
  3. What genres, ratings (audiences) and durations dominate, and what is growing?
  4. What content is available in different countries, and which markets are rising?
  5. Who are the most frequent actors and directors by content type and market?
  6. What is the best time (month / day) to launch a TV show or movie?

Approach. Clean the data → profile it (shape, types, missing values, statistics) → un-nest multi-value columns (cast, director, country, genre) → univariate & bivariate visuals → outlier checks → convert patterns into business insights and plain-language recommendations.

Important caveat: the data describes what is on Netflix, not what people watch. Viewing hours, ratings and revenue are not available, so "more titles" means "more investment/supply", not necessarily "more demand". 2021 only covers January to 25 September.

Observations

  • The dataset has 8,807 rows × 12 columns; each row is one unique title (no duplicate rows or IDs). After trimming stray spaces, one title (Consequences, a 2014 Turkish movie) appears twice, which is a negligible duplicate listing.
  • Only release_year is numeric (int64). Everything else is text (object/str), including date_added (should be a date) and duration (mixes "90 min" and "2 Seasons", so it needs splitting into a number and a unit).
  • cast, director, country and listed_in hold comma-separated lists (e.g. several actors per title), so they must be un-nested before counting.

4. Data cleaning & feature engineering¶

4.1 Fixing a data-entry error. Three Louis C.K. stand-up specials have their duration typed into the rating column.

display(df.loc[bad, ['title', 'type', 'rating', 'duration']])
df.loc[bad, 'duration'] = df.loc[bad, 'rating']   # move the value to the right column
df.loc[bad, 'rating'] = np.nan                    # the true rating is unknown

4.2 Trimming text, parsing dates and splitting duration into a number + unit; creating time and audience features.

In [5]:
for col in ['type', 'title', 'director', 'cast', 'country', 'date_added', 'rating', 'duration', 'listed_in']:
    df[col] = df[col].str.strip()

df['date_added']   = pd.to_datetime(df['date_added'], format='%B %d, %Y', errors='coerce')
df['year_added']   = df['date_added'].dt.year.astype('Int64')
df['month_added']  = df['date_added'].dt.month.astype('Int64')
df['month_name']   = df['date_added'].dt.month_name().str[:3]
df['weekday_added']= df['date_added'].dt.day_name()
df['day_added']    = df['date_added'].dt.day.astype('Int64')

df['duration_num']  = df['duration'].str.extract(r'(\d+)').astype(float)
df['duration_unit'] = np.where(df['duration'].str.contains('Season', na=False), 'Seasons', 'Minutes')

# How many years after release did the title reach Netflix?
df['years_to_netflix'] = df['year_added'] - df['release_year']

# Audience group: maps 14 rating codes to 4 groups a business reader understands
audience = {'TV-Y': 'Little Kids', 'TV-G': 'Little Kids', 'G': 'Little Kids',
            'TV-Y7': 'Older Kids', 'TV-Y7-FV': 'Older Kids', 'PG': 'Older Kids', 'TV-PG': 'Older Kids',
            'PG-13': 'Teens', 'TV-14': 'Teens',
            'R': 'Adults', 'NC-17': 'Adults', 'TV-MA': 'Adults',
            'NR': 'Unrated', 'UR': 'Unrated'}
df['audience'] = df['rating'].map(audience)

# Release era for coarse comparisons
df['release_era'] = pd.cut(df['release_year'], [1900, 1989, 1999, 2009, 2015, 2021],
                           labels=['Before 1990', '1990s', '2000s', '2010–15', '2016–21'])

4.3 Converting categorical attributes to the category dtype (saves memory and fixes a logical order for ratings and audiences).

In [6]:
before = df.memory_usage(deep=True).sum() / 1024**2
rating_order = ['TV-Y', 'TV-Y7', 'TV-Y7-FV', 'TV-G', 'G', 'TV-PG', 'PG', 'PG-13', 'TV-14', 'R', 'TV-MA', 'NC-17', 'NR', 'UR']
df['type']          = df['type'].astype('category')
df['rating']        = pd.Categorical(df['rating'], categories=rating_order, ordered=True)
df['audience']      = pd.Categorical(df['audience'], categories=['Little Kids', 'Older Kids', 'Teens', 'Adults', 'Unrated'], ordered=True)
df['duration_unit'] = df['duration_unit'].astype('category')
df['weekday_added'] = pd.Categorical(df['weekday_added'], categories=['Monday','Tuesday','Wednesday','Thursday','Friday','Saturday','Sunday'], ordered=True)
after = df.memory_usage(deep=True).sum() / 1024**2
print(f'Memory: {before:.2f} MB -> {after:.2f} MB')

Observations

  • type, rating, audience, duration_unit and weekday_added are now category (ordered where order matters, e.g. ratings go from youngest to most mature audience).
  • date_added is a real date, so we can analyse trends by year, month and weekday.
  • duration is split into duration_num (minutes for movies, seasons for TV) + duration_unit. Movies and TV are therefore analysed separately for duration; mixing minutes and seasons would be meaningless.
  • New features: year_added, month_added, weekday_added, years_to_netflix, audience, release_era.

Observations

  • director is the biggest gap (29.9%), but this is mostly structural: 91% of TV shows have no director (TV is directed per episode), versus only 3% of movies.
  • cast (9.4%) and country (9.4%) are moderately missing; TV shows are missing them about twice as often as movies.
  • date_added (10 rows, all TV shows), rating (7) and duration (0 after the fix) are negligible.

Treatment (no rows dropped, so no information is lost):

  • director, cast, country → filled with "Unknown" for value counts; "Unknown" is excluded from "Top-N" rankings so it does not distort them.
  • rating → "Unknown" isn't a rating code, so the 7 rows are left as missing (category NaN) and simply ignored in rating plots.
  • date_added → 10 rows left missing and ignored in time-based charts (0.1% of data).

6.1 Comments on the range of attributes

  • release_year spans 1925–2021 (96 years) but is heavily concentrated in recent years: median 2017, the middle 50% fall in 2013–2019, and 84.8% of titles were released in 2010 or later. Netflix is a recent-content platform; the classic catalogue is thin.
  • date_added spans Jan 2008 – 25 Sep 2021, but meaningful volumes only start in 2015–16, the years of Netflix's global expansion.
  • Movie duration ranges from 3 to 312 minutes; mean 99.6 vs median 98, so the distribution is close to symmetric with long tails on both ends (shorts and epics).
  • TV seasons range from 1 to 17, but the median is 1 and the mean only 1.76, i.e. strongly right-skewed.
  • years_to_netflix ranges from −3 to 93 years. Negative values (14 titles) are data-entry inconsistencies or titles listed before their official release year; the median is just 1 year, so most content reaches Netflix very quickly.
  • Categorical cardinality: 2 types, 14 ratings, 748 raw country combinations (749 incl. "Unknown") (122 real countries after un-nesting), 514 genre combinations (42 genres), 4,528 director strings and 7,692 cast strings, which is why un-nesting is essential.
  • The most frequent single values: type = Movie (6,131), rating = TV-MA (3,207), country = United States (2,818 single-country titles), genre string = "Dramas, International Movies".

Observations

  • Type: 69.6% movies (6,131) vs 30.4% TV shows (2,676), roughly 2.3 movies for every TV show.
  • Rating: TV-MA (36.4%) and TV-14 (24.5%) together make up 61% of the catalogue. Grouped by audience, Adults ≈ 46% and Teens ≈ 30%, while Little Kids is only 6.5% and Older Kids 17%.
  • Release era: the 2016–21 window alone holds 64% of all titles (and 2010–15 another 21%), while pre-1990 titles are under 3%, confirming the focus on fresh content.
  • TV seasons: "1 Season" is by far the most common value (1,793 shows, 67%); only ~9% of shows have 4+ seasons.
  • Movie durations: the most common runtimes are 90–97 minutes.
  • Additions per year: volumes explode from 82 (2015) to 429 (2016) to 1,188 (2017), peak at 2,016 in 2019, then dip in 2020 (1,879). 2021 is a partial year (1,498 by late September).

8. Pre-processing: un-nesting cast, director, country & genre¶

A title like "Dramas, International Movies" belongs to both genres, and a film with 10 actors credits all 10. We split each list and give every value its own row (explode). Each un-nested table keeps show_id, so it can be joined back to any attribute.

In [14]:
def unnest(frame, col):
    'Split a comma-separated column into one row per value, keeping the title attributes.'
    out = frame[['show_id', 'type', 'title', 'release_year', 'year_added', 'rating', 'audience', 'duration_num', col]].copy()
    out[col] = out[col].str.split(',')
    out = out.explode(col).reset_index(drop=True)
    out[col] = out[col].str.strip()
    return out[out[col].notna() & (out[col] != '')]

df_cast     = unnest(df, 'cast')
df_director = unnest(df, 'director')
df_country  = unnest(df, 'country')
df_genre    = unnest(df, 'listed_in').rename(columns={'listed_in': 'genre'})

known = lambda d, c: d[d[c] != 'Unknown']
summary = pd.DataFrame({
    'rows after un-nesting': [len(df_cast), len(df_director), len(df_country), len(df_genre)],
    'unique values': [known(df_cast,'cast')['cast'].nunique(), known(df_director,'director')['director'].nunique(),
                      known(df_country,'country')['country'].nunique(), df_genre['genre'].nunique()]},
    index=['cast', 'director', 'country', 'genre'])
display(summary)
co = known(df_country, 'country').groupby('show_id').size()
print(f'Titles produced by 2+ countries (co-productions): {(co > 1).sum():,}')
print(f'Average genres per title: {len(df_genre) / len(df):.2f}  |  Average cast per title (known): {len(known(df_cast,"cast")) / (df.cast != "Unknown").sum():.1f}')

['netflix_cast_unnested.csv', 'netflix_cleaned.csv', 'netflix_country_unnested.csv', 'netflix_director_unnested.csv', 'netflix_genre_unnested.csv']

Observations

  • After un-nesting there are 122 countries, 42 genres, ~36,400 actors and ~5,000 directors.
  • 1,315 titles (15%) are co-productions between two or more countries, a sign that Netflix uses partnerships to enter markets.
  • The average title is tagged with ~2.2 genres and lists ~8 cast members, so un-nested counts add up to more than the number of titles.
  • The United States leads every country ranking, but India is a clear #2 and Indian actors (Anupam Kher, Shah Rukh Khan, Naseeruddin Shah) dominate the top-actor list.

9. Univariate visual analysis¶

9.1 Movies vs TV shows (countplot)¶

In [17]:
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.4))
order = ['Movie', 'TV Show']
sns.countplot(data=df, x='type', order=order, palette=PAL, width=0.55, ax=ax)
for p, t in zip(ax.patches, order):
    n = (df.type == t).sum(); ax.annotate(f'{n:,}  ({n/len(df):.0%})', (p.get_x()+p.get_width()/2, p.get_height()), ha='center', va='bottom', fontsize=10, xytext=(0, 3), textcoords='offset points')
ax.set(title='Netflix catalogue: movies vs TV shows', xlabel='', ylabel='Number of titles', ylim=(0, 7000))
sns.despine(); save('02_type_count')

Insight: Movies make up 70% of the catalogue (6,131) vs 30% for TV shows (2,676). Netflix's library is built on movies, yet TV shows are what keep subscribers returning month after month (multi-episode viewing), so this mix is worth watching over time (see 10.1).

9.2 Release year distribution (distplot / histogram with KDE)¶

In [18]:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.6))
sns.histplot(df['release_year'], bins=50, kde=True, color=MUTED, ax=axes[0])
axes[0].set(title='Release year: all titles (1925–2021)', xlabel='Release year', ylabel='Titles')
sns.histplot(data=df[df.release_year >= 1990], x='release_year', hue='type', palette=PAL, binwidth=1,
             kde=True, element='step', alpha=0.25, ax=axes[1])
axes[1].set(title='Release year since 1990, by type', xlabel='Release year', ylabel='Titles')
sns.despine(); save('03_release_year_dist')

Insights

  • The distribution is strongly left-skewed: a long thin tail back to 1925 and a sharp peak in 2017–2018. Half of all titles were released in 2017 or later.
  • Movies peak in 2017–2018 (767 each); TV shows keep rising until 2020 (436). In 2021 there are already more TV shows (315) than movies (277) by release year.
  • The drop in 2020–21 is partly COVID-related production delays and partly because the data stops in September 2021.

9.3 Movie duration (distplot + boxplot) and TV seasons (countplot)¶

In [19]:
movies, shows = df[df.type == 'Movie'], df[df.type == 'TV Show']
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.6), gridspec_kw={'width_ratios': [1.4, 1]})
sns.histplot(movies['duration_num'], bins=60, kde=True, color=MOVIE, ax=axes[0])
med = movies['duration_num'].median()
axes[0].axvline(med, color=INK, ls='--', lw=1.2); axes[0].text(med + 4, axes[0].get_ylim()[1]*0.9, f'median {med:.0f} min', fontsize=9)
axes[0].set(title='Movie duration (minutes)', xlabel='Minutes', ylabel='Movies')
s = shows['duration_num'].value_counts().sort_index()
axes[1].bar(s.index.astype(int).astype(str), s.values, color=TV, width=0.7)
axes[1].set(title='TV shows by number of seasons', xlabel='Seasons', ylabel='TV shows')
for i, v in enumerate(s.values[:4]): axes[1].text(i, v + 20, f'{v/len(shows):.0%}', ha='center', fontsize=8)
sns.despine(); save('04_duration_dist')

Insights

  • Movie runtimes are bell-shaped around 90–110 minutes (median 98, mean 99.6). The middle 50% run 87–114 min. Short films / stand-up (<60 min) and epics (>150 min, mostly Indian films) form the tails.
  • TV is the opposite shape: 67% of shows have 1 season, 16% have 2 and the share keeps halving. Few shows earn renewals, either because Netflix cancels early or because many are limited series / licensed single seasons.

9.4 Ratings & audience groups (countplot)¶

In [20]:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.6), gridspec_kw={'width_ratios': [1.6, 1]})
r = df['rating'].value_counts().reindex(rating_order)
axes[0].bar(r.index, r.values, color=[MOVIE if x in ('TV-MA','R','NC-17') else MUTED for x in r.index], width=0.7)
axes[0].set(title='Titles by rating (red = adult ratings)', ylabel='Titles'); axes[0].tick_params(axis='x', rotation=45)
label_bars(axes[0])
a = df['audience'].value_counts().reindex(['Little Kids', 'Older Kids', 'Teens', 'Adults', 'Unrated'])
axes[1].barh(a.index[::-1], a.values[::-1], color=MUTED, height=0.6)
for i, v in enumerate(a.values[::-1]): axes[1].text(v + 40, i, f'{v/a.sum():.0%}', va='center', fontsize=9)
axes[1].set(title='Titles by audience group', xlabel='Titles', xlim=(0, 4800))
sns.despine(); save('05_ratings')

Insights

  • TV-MA (3,207) is the single largest rating, followed by TV-14 (2,160). Adult-rated titles (TV-MA, R, NC-17) make up ~46% of the catalogue.
  • Little Kids content is only 6.5% and older kids 17%. Families are a large subscriber segment, so this is a potential gap.
  • Movie-style ratings (G, PG, PG-13, R) are much rarer than TV ratings, because most Netflix content is rated under the TV system, including movies.

9.5 Top countries & genres (countplot of un-nested data)¶

In [21]:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.2))
c = known(df_country, 'country')['country'].value_counts().head(12)
axes[0].barh(c.index[::-1], c.values[::-1], color=[MOVIE if i < 3 else MUTED for i in range(len(c))][::-1], height=0.65)
axes[0].set(title='Top 12 producing countries', xlabel='Titles'); label_bars(axes[0])

sns.despine(); save('06_top_countries_genres')

Insights

  • The US (3,690) is ~3.5× India (1,046), and the top 3 (US, India, UK) account for more than half of all country credits. Canada, France, Japan, Spain, South Korea and Germany form a second tier with 200–450 titles each.
  • "International Movies" (2,752) and "Dramas" (2,427) are the biggest genres, followed by Comedies (1,674). Netflix's identity is drama + non-English content, while documentaries and action are mid-sized.

9.6 When are titles added? (countplots by year, month, weekday)¶

In [22]:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(13, 3.4))
y = df['year_added'].value_counts().sort_index().loc[2014:]
axes[0].bar(y.index.astype(str), y.values, color=MUTED, width=0.7); axes[0].set(title='Titles added per year', ylabel='Titles')
axes[0].tick_params(axis='x', rotation=45); axes[0].text(len(y)-1, y.iloc[-1] + 40, 'to Sep', ha='center', fontsize=8)
m = df['month_added'].value_counts().sort_index()
axes[1].bar(pd.to_datetime(m.index.astype(int), format='%m').strftime('%b'), m.values, color=[MOVIE if v >= m.nlargest(3).min() else MUTED for v in m.values], width=0.7)
axes[1].set(title='Titles added by month (all years)'); axes[1].tick_params(axis='x', rotation=45)
w = df['weekday_added'].value_counts().sort_index()
axes[2].bar(w.index.str[:3], w.values, color=[MOVIE if d == 'Friday' else MUTED for d in w.index], width=0.7)
axes[2].set(title='Titles added by weekday')
sns.despine(); save('07_when_added')

Insights

  • Additions grew ~25× from 2015 to 2019, then dipped 7% in 2020 (COVID production shutdowns). The 2021 bar covers only ~8.8 months; at its run-rate (~170/month) 2021 would land around 2,000, roughly flat versus 2019–20. Growth has plateaued.
  • By month, additions are fairly even, but July (827), December (813) and September (770) are the strongest; February (563) is the weakest month.
  • Friday is the launch day by far (~28% of all additions), almost double any other weekday, which lines up with weekend binge-watching. The 1st of the month is also a major drop date (2,212 titles), because licensing deals usually start on the 1st.

10. Bivariate & multivariate visual analysis¶

10.1 Is Netflix focusing more on TV shows in recent years?¶

In [23]:
t = pd.crosstab(df['year_added'], df['type']).loc[2015:]
share = (t['TV Show'] / t.sum(axis=1) * 100)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.6))
for col in ['Movie', 'TV Show']:
    axes[0].plot(t.index.astype(int), t[col], marker='o', lw=2, ms=6, color=PAL[col], label=col)
    axes[0].text(2021.15, t[col].iloc[-1], col, color=PAL[col], va='center', fontsize=9)
axes[0].set(title='Titles added per year by type', ylabel='Titles added', xlim=(2014.7, 2021.9)); axes[0].legend(loc='upper left', frameon=False)
axes[1].plot(share.index.astype(int), share.values, marker='o', lw=2, ms=6, color=TV)
for x, v in share.items(): axes[1].text(x, v + 1, f'{v:.0f}%', ha='center', fontsize=8)
axes[1].set(title='TV shows as % of titles added', ylabel='% TV shows', ylim=(15, 50))
axes[1].yaxis.set_major_formatter(mtick.PercentFormatter(decimals=0))
sns.despine(); save('08_tv_vs_movie_trend')

Insights

  • Yes, the shift to TV is real. After a 2016 spike (41%, the global-launch catalogue), the TV share fell to 25% in 2018 and has climbed every year since: 29% → 32% → 34% (2021).
  • Movie additions fell 10% from 2019 to 2020 (1,424 → 1,284) while TV additions held flat (592 → 595). Netflix protected its TV pipeline even as overall additions slowed.

10.2 How has the number of releases changed over the last 30 years? (release year × type)¶

In [24]:
r = pd.crosstab(df['release_year'], df['type']).loc[1991:2021]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 3.4))
for col in ['Movie', 'TV Show']:
    ax.plot(r.index, r[col], lw=2, color=PAL[col], label=col)
    ax.text(2021.3, r[col].iloc[-1], col, color=PAL[col], va='bottom' if col == 'TV Show' else 'top', fontsize=9)
ax.axvspan(2019.5, 2021, color='#f3f3f1'); ax.text(2019.6, r.values.max()*0.92, 'COVID +\npartial 2021', fontsize=8, color='#52514e')
ax.set(title='Titles on Netflix by original release year (1991–2021)', xlabel='Release year', ylabel='Titles', xlim=(1991, 2023))

display(r.loc[[1991, 2001, 2011, 2016, 2018, 2020, 2021]].T)
release_year 1991 2001 2011 2016 2018 2020 2021
type
Movie 16 40 145 658 767 517 277
TV Show 1 5 40 244 380 436 315

Insights

  • Titles from the 1990s are scarce (20–35 movies per year). Growth accelerates after 2008 and explodes after 2014: movies released in 2018 (767) outnumber those from 2008 (113) almost 7 to 1.
  • Movies peaked with 2017–18 releases and have declined since; TV shows grew every year up to 2020 and overtook movies for 2021 releases. Netflix's newest content is increasingly episodic.

10.3 What content is available in different countries? (country × type, country × genre)¶

In [25]:
top10 = known(df_country, 'country')['country'].value_counts().head(10).index
ct = pd.crosstab(df_country['country'], df_country['type']).loc[top10]
ctp = ct.div(ct.sum(axis=1), axis=0) * 100
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 3.8))
ax.barh(ctp.index[::-1], ctp['Movie'][::-1], color=MOVIE, label='Movie', height=0.65, edgecolor='white', linewidth=2)
ax.barh(ctp.index[::-1], ctp['TV Show'][::-1], left=ctp['Movie'][::-1], color=TV, label='TV Show', height=0.65, edgecolor='white', linewidth=2)
for i, (mv_, n) in enumerate(zip(ctp['Movie'][::-1], ct.sum(axis=1)[::-1])):
    ax.text(2, i, f'{mv_:.0f}%', va='center', color='white', fontsize=8, fontweight='bold')
    ax.text(101, i, f'n={n:,}', va='center', fontsize=8, color='#52514e')
ax.set(title='Movie vs TV mix in the top 10 producing countries', xlabel='% of titles', xlim=(0, 112))
ax.set_title(ax.get_title(), pad=24); ax.legend(frameon=False, ncol=2, loc='lower center', bbox_to_anchor=(0.45, 1.0)); sns.despine(left=True); save('10_country_type_mix')

Insights

  • India is 92% movies, the most movie-centric major market (Bollywood). Egypt, Hong Kong and Nigeria (not shown) are similar.
  • Japan (63% TV) and South Korea (74% TV) are the only top-10 markets where TV dominates, driven by anime and K-dramas.
  • The UK (34% TV) is more TV-oriented than the US (25%), reflecting its strength in British series.
In [26]:
cg = known(df_country, 'country')[['show_id', 'country']].merge(df_genre[['show_id', 'genre']], on='show_id')
top_genres = df_genre['genre'].value_counts().head(14).index
heat = pd.crosstab(cg['country'], cg['genre']).loc[top10, top_genres]
heat_pct = heat.div(heat.sum(axis=1), axis=0) * 100
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 4.6))
sns.heatmap(heat_pct, annot=True, fmt='.0f', cmap='Reds', linewidths=1, linecolor='white', cbar_kws={'label': '% of country\'s genre tags'}, ax=ax, annot_kws={'size': 8})
ax.set(title='Genre mix by country (% of each country\'s genre tags)', xlabel='', ylabel='')
plt.xticks(rotation=40, ha='right'); save('11_country_genre_heatmap')

Insights

  • US: the most balanced mix: Dramas (17%), Comedies (14%), Documentaries (11%) and Children & Family (8%), with almost no "International" tag (it is the home market). A "something for everyone" market.
  • India: International Movies (34%) + Dramas (26%) + Comedies (13%) make up 73% of tags; documentaries, kids' and TV genres are ~1% each, so there is clear room to diversify.
  • UK: balanced between movies and TV, with a strong Documentaries (11%) share, equal to the US.
  • Japan: International TV (35%) and Action & Adventure (13%), the highest action share of any market, driven by anime (anime genres sit just outside this top-14 view).
  • South Korea: International TV (40%) and TV Dramas (10%): the K-drama factory.
  • Canada: the highest Children & Family (12%) and Kids' TV (9%) shares, a known animation hub.
  • Mexico & Spain: Crime TV (Mexico 11%, Spain 6%) and Thrillers (Spain 8%) are well above average, so crime/thriller is a proven Spanish-language strength.

country
United States 462 600 856 828 627
India 162 349 218 199 105
United Kingdom 134 147 191 146 120

Spain 42 43 53 43 33

Insights (2021 is January–September only)

  • India peaked in 2018 (349 titles) and fell by ~43% in 2020 (199). After an early licensing push, Indian additions slowed; the opportunity now is quality originals rather than volume.
  • Japan (44 → 79) and South Korea (33 → 56) grew 70–80% from 2018 to 2020, riding global demand for anime and K-dramas.
  • Nigeria (1 → 42) and Egypt (3 → 54) went from almost nothing in 2018 to meaningful volumes by 2020: new growth frontiers in Africa and the Middle East. Nigeria kept going in 2021 (28 by September), while Egypt's 2019–20 jump was a one-off batch (only 7 in 2021). Spain is steady (33–53 titles a year) and Turkey recovered to 26–28 a year after a dip in 2018.

10.5 Which genres are growing? (genre × year added)¶

In [28]:
gy = df_genre.dropna(subset=['year_added']); gy = pd.crosstab(gy['genre'], gy['year_added'].astype(int))
sel = ['Reality TV', "Kids' TV", 'Children & Family Movies', 'Romantic Movies', 'TV Comedies', 'Action & Adventure', 'Thrillers',
       'Documentaries', 'Stand-Up Comedy', 'Independent Movies']
idx = (gy.loc[sel, 2020] / gy.loc[sel, 2018] * 100 - 100).sort_values()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 3.6))
ax.barh(idx.index, idx.values, color=[TV if v > 0 else MOVIE for v in idx.values], height=0.6)
for i, v in enumerate(idx.values): ax.text(v + (3 if v > 0 else -3), i, f'{v:+.0f}%', va='center', ha='left' if v > 0 else 'right', fontsize=9)
ax.axvline(0, color=INK, lw=0.8); ax.set(title='Change in titles added per genre, 2018 → 2020', xlabel='% change', xlim=(-80, 130))
sns.despine(left=True); save('13_genre_growth')

Insights

  • Fastest-growing genres: Reality TV (+95%), Children & Family Movies (+100%), Kids' TV (+66%), Romantic Movies (+60%) and TV Comedies (+26%). Netflix is clearly building family, light-entertainment and unscripted content.
  • Shrinking genres: Stand-Up Comedy (−46%), Documentaries (−29%) and Independent Movies (−9%).
  • Action & Adventure dipped in 2020 but by September 2021 had already passed its 2020 total (196 vs 170), a signal of renewed blockbuster investment.

10.6 Genres for movies vs TV shows¶

In [29]:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 3.8))
for ax, t_, col in [(axes[0], 'Movie', MOVIE), (axes[1], 'TV Show', TV)]:
    s = df_genre.loc[df_genre.type == t_, 'genre'].value_counts().head(10)
    ax.barh(s.index[::-1], s.values[::-1], color=col, height=0.65); label_bars(ax)
    ax.set(title=f'Top 10 genres: {t_}s', xlabel='Titles')
sns.despine(); save('14_genres_by_type')

Insights

  • Movies: International (2,752), Dramas (2,427) and Comedies (1,674) lead, then Documentaries, Action, Independent and Children & Family.
  • TV: International TV (1,351), TV Dramas (763), TV Comedies (581), then Crime TV (470) and Kids' TV (451). Crime is notably stronger on TV than thrillers are among movies, a natural fit for multi-episode storytelling.
  • Both formats share a core of international + drama + comedy; TV adds Crime, Kids, Docuseries, Reality and Anime (176) as distinct niches.

  • Duration rises with audience age. Kids' movies (TV-Y median 46 min, TV-Y7 68 min) are far shorter than teen/adult films (PG-13 106, TV-14 107, R 103 min).

Insights

  • Stand-Up Comedy (median ~65 min), Documentaries (~86) and Children & Family (~87) are the shortest formats, which makes them cheap, fast and good "filler" between big releases.
  • Dramas (~109), Action & Adventure (~108), International (~107) and Romantic Movies (~107) run longest; international films carry the largest high-end outliers (3-hour Indian epics).

type Movie TV Show
release_year 2016.0 2018.0
years_to_netflix 2.0 0.0

Insights

  • TV shows are newer: median release year 2018 vs 2016 for movies; the movie box is much taller, with outliers back to the 1940s.
  • TV shows reach Netflix in the same year (median 0 years), which is consistent with Netflix originals and simultaneous releases. Movies arrive ~2 years after release on median (after cinema and other windows), with many older catalogue films.
  • Practical meaning: Netflix's TV slate is fresh and largely self-produced; its movie slate depends more on licensing older titles.

10.9 Ratings / audiences by content type¶

In [33]:

Insights

  • Both formats are adult-heavy (47% of movies, 43% of TV), but TV has twice the little-kids share (10% vs 5%), and Little + Older Kids ≈ 30% of TV vs 21% of movies. Kids' content works better as series (repeat viewing, short episodes).
  • Teens (PG-13 / TV-14) are ~31% of movies and ~27% of TV.

ym.columns = pd.to_datetime(ym.columns.astype(int), format='%m').strftime('%b')
sns.heatmap(ym, cmap='Reds', annot=True, fmt='.0f', linewidths=1, linecolor='white', annot_kws={'size': 7}, cbar=False, ax=axes[1])
axes[1].set(title='Titles added: year × month', xlabel='', ylabel='')
sns.despine(ax=axes[0]); save('19_best_launch_month')

Insights: best time to launch

  • TV shows: the highest shares are in December (~10%) and July (~10%), followed by September; February is the weakest (~7%). These match the year-end holidays and summer vacations, when people have time to binge.
  • Movies: strongest in July, April, December and January; also weakest in February.
  • Weekday: 35% of TV shows and ~26% of movies are added on a Friday, the single best day to set up a weekend binge.
  • The heatmap shows Q4 (Oct–Dec) was the hottest period in 2018 and 2019 (Nov 2019 = 255 titles), while in 2021 Netflix front-loaded the summer: July 2021 (257) is the single biggest month on record. Year-end and mid-summer are consistently strong.

Insights

  • release_year and years_to_netflix are almost perfectly negatively correlated (−0.99), which is expected: older films have, by definition, waited longer to reach Netflix.
  • Movie duration has a weak negative relationship with release year (−0.21): the median runtime falls from ~112–118 min for 1970s–80s films to ~107 min in the 2000s and ~95–97 min since 2015. Newer releases are getting shorter, matching streaming viewing habits.
  • year_added is only weakly related to duration (0.13), so the length of what Netflix acquires has barely changed over time.

11. Outlier check (IQR method)¶

In [39]:
def iqr_report(s, name):
    q1, q3 = s.quantile([.25, .75]); iqr = q3 - q1; lo, hi = q1 - 1.5 * iqr, q3 + 1.5 * iqr
    out = s[(s < lo) | (s > hi)]
    return pd.Series({'Q1': q1, 'Q3': q3, 'IQR': iqr, 'lower fence': lo, 'upper fence': hi,
                      'outliers': len(out), '% outliers': round(len(out) / s.notna().sum() * 100, 1), 'min': s.min(), 'max': s.max()}, name=name)

rep = pd.concat([iqr_report(movies['duration_num'], 'Movie duration (min)'),
                 iqr_report(shows['duration_num'], 'TV seasons'),
                 iqr_report(df['release_year'].astype(float), 'Release year'),
                 iqr_report(df['years_to_netflix'].astype(float), 'Years to Netflix')], axis=1).T
display(rep.round(1))

Observations & treatment

  • Movie duration: ~450 movies (7%) fall outside 46.5–154.5 min. Short ones are stand-up specials, kids' shorts and short documentaries; long ones are mostly Indian films and epics (Black Mirror: Bandersnatch at 312 min is interactive). These are real titles, not errors, so they are kept, and medians (not means) are reported.
  • TV seasons: anything over 3 seasons is a statistical "outlier" because 67% of shows have one season. Long-running hits (e.g. Grey's Anatomy, 17 seasons) are valuable, not errors, so they are kept.
  • Release year: with the middle 50% between 2013 and 2019, any title released before 2004 is a statistical outlier (719 titles, 8%); kept because they represent the classic catalogue.
  • Years to Netflix: negative values (14 rows) are genuine data inconsistencies and should be ignored in lag analysis; large positive values are classic films and are kept.
  • Conclusion: no outlier removal is needed for this descriptive analysis; robust statistics (median, IQR) are used where skew matters.

12. Business insights¶

  1. Netflix is pivoting towards TV. TV's share of new additions rose for three straight years (25% → 34%), and for 2021 releases TV shows outnumber movies (315 vs 277). Series drive repeat engagement and subscriber retention, and Netflix's own investment pattern confirms it.
  2. Growth has plateaued. Additions peaked at 2,016 titles in 2019, then slowed in 2020–21 (COVID production halts, rising content costs). Future growth must come from better targeting, not just more titles.
  3. The catalogue is adult-first, with a family gap. ~46% of titles are adult-rated and only 6.5% are for little kids, yet Children & Family movies doubled (+100%) and Kids' TV grew +66% in 2018–20. Netflix itself is moving into this gap.
  4. International content is the core of the brand. "International Movies/TV Shows" are the #1 genre for both formats; 15% of titles are co-productions across countries. Mexico and Spain over-index on crime and thrillers; Canada on kids' animation.
  5. Each market has a distinct taste profile:
    • India: movies (92%), dramas & comedies, Bollywood star-driven; additions fell 43% from the 2018 peak.
    • Japan: anime-led TV (63% TV); Japanese voice actors are the most frequent TV cast.
    • South Korea: K-drama/romantic TV (74% TV), additions nearly doubled 2018→2019.
    • UK: British series and documentaries. US: the broadest mix, strongest in docs, comedy and kids.
    • Nigeria & Egypt: went from almost zero to 42–54 titles/year within two years (Nigeria still growing in 2021).
  6. Short-lived TV is the norm. Two-thirds of shows end after one season, which signals high experimentation (many pilots, few renewals) and limited series formats.
  7. Ideal movie length is clear. Most movies are 87–114 min; kids' content is far shorter (46–68 min), and stand-up/docs fill the 60–90 min band cheaply.
  8. Release timing is deliberate. Friday launches (28% overall, 35% of TV) and 1st-of-month licensing drops dominate; July and December are the peak months for TV, and February is the quietest.
  9. Original TV vs licensed movies. TV arrives on Netflix in the same year it is released (median 0 years), consistent with originals, while movies arrive ~2 years later, consistent with licensing windows.
  10. Growing vs declining genres. Reality TV (+95%), romantic movies (+60%) and kids' content are rising; stand-up (−46%) and documentaries (−29%) are shrinking.

13. Recommendations (simple action items)¶

  1. Make more TV series. Keep raising the share of TV shows, especially international dramas, crime series and kids' shows. Series keep people subscribed month after month.
  2. Give good shows a second season. Two out of three shows stop after season 1. Set clear rules for renewing shows that people finish, so popular stories can grow into long-running hits.
  3. Build more family and kids' content. Content for little kids is only about 1 in 15 titles, yet kids and family is one of the fastest-growing areas. Add more animated series and family films, especially from India and Canada, where there is proven talent.
  4. Go local, country by country:
    • India: keep making movies with popular local stars, and start testing Indian web-series to move beyond films.
    • Japan: invest in anime series that can travel worldwide.
    • South Korea: keep funding K-dramas and romance series; this market's output nearly doubled in a year.
    • Mexico and Spain: make more Spanish-language crime and thriller series, a proven strength there.
    • Nigeria and Egypt: the fastest-growing new markets. Partner with local studios to produce more local movies and series there.
    • UK: keep investing in British dramas and nature/documentary series.
  5. Keep movies around 90 to 110 minutes. That is where most successful Netflix movies sit. Kids' movies can be shorter (around an hour).
  6. Launch big shows on a Friday, in July or December. These are the months when most TV shows go live and people have holiday time to binge. Avoid February for big launches, or use it for smaller titles.
  7. Grow the right genres. Put more money into reality shows, romance, action and kids' content, which are all growing. Spend carefully on stand-up specials and documentaries, which Netflix is already adding less of.
  8. Co-produce to enter new markets. 15% of titles are made by two or more countries. Partnering with local producers lowers cost and risk and speeds up entry into new countries.
  9. Refresh the classic movie library selectively. Older films make up a small share; adding well-known classics can attract older audiences at low cost.
  10. Track what people watch, not just what is added. Pair this catalogue view with viewing data so these bets can be measured and adjusted every quarter.
